note: Recent arXiv papers, broken down from their abstracts. Each entry says what the authors claim, not more. status is the authors' own comment line. New entries are added by the daily digest job; the newest are first.

papers.t: The JWST Sub-Jupiters Survey: Observed Sensitivities to the Wide-Separation, Cold, Sub-Jupiter Exoplanet Population
papers.by: Giovanni M. Strampelli, Aarynn L. Carter, Beth Biller and 32 others
papers.status: 40 pages, 17 figures, 8 tables. Accepted for publication at AJ
papers.one: We find that these programs are sensitive to sub-Saturn to Jupiter mass exoplanets with effective temperature (Tₑff) as low as ≲ 250 K, already at ~2 arcsec.
papers.q: A comparison with the SHINE survey confirms that the improvements in mass sensitivity provided by JWST high-contrast imaging surveys outpace current ground observation for masses ≲ 1 M_J and separations between ~20-500 au, opening up a novel parameter space to explore. Overall, this analysis provides a robust framework for interpreting future exoplanet detections.
papers.how: We present a sensitivity analysis of three recent JWST direct imaging programs (GO-4050, GO-5835, and SURVEY-6005) designed to build a demographic study of sub-Jupiter mass ($0.1 - 1$ M_J) exoplanets in nearby young associations and moving groups.

papers.t: Unexpected Plateau: The Constant logε(Th/Eu) Ratio of Actinide-Boost Stars
papers.by: J. Shejeelammal, Asa Skuladottir, Marta Molero and 4 others
papers.one: Combined with other evidence, our results suggest that mergers with neutron stars are the most promising astrophysical site for actinide-boost stars.
papers.q: The astrophysical site of the rapid neutron-capture process (r-process) is still one of the major open questions in astronomy. A key mystery is the origin of the peculiar actinide-to-lanthanide ratio found in the so called actinide-boost stars, with logε(Th/Eu)>-0.35.
papers.how: Here we present the largest sample of Th measurements in stars formed in an external galaxy, Gaia Sausage Enceladus. From this sample, we present the three most metal-rich actinide-boost stars discovered to date, -1.6<[Fe/H]<-1.1.
found: Unexpectedly, actinide-boost stars lie on a very narrow (σ=0.02) plateau of logε(Th/Eu)=-0.2, clearly separated from actinide-normal stars.
Chemical evolution models show that such a plateau can arise, even at [Fe/H] = -1, when a single actinide-rich event dominates the r-process content of a small or gas-depleted system.

papers.t: The Velocity Curves and Three-Dimensional Kinematics of the Milky Way from Gaia DR3
papers.status: 19 pages, 17 figures, 4 tables. Published in Galaxies 2026, 14(6), 101
papers.one: To facilitate the description of the observations, we employ a simplified axisymmetric Monte Carlo model with several free parameters that reproduces the main kinematic trends.
papers.q: From these data, we determine the local solar velocity (U☉,V☉,W☉) = (10.5±0.7,14.5±0.9,7.33±0.1) ~km/s, the average rotation velocity\linebreak V₀ = (228±4) km/s, and the circular velocity V_c = (234±4) {km/s,} both at the radius R☉. Next, within the range of 3-14 kpc, we derive the Galactic circular velocity curve V_c(R) and determine the average spherical components of the stellar velocities as functions of both Galactocentric radius R and distance from the Galactic plane vertZvert.
papers.how: We investigate the fundamental kinematic parameters of stellar motions in the Milky Way using a statistical sample of 27,485,720 stars with measured three-dimensional velocities from the Gaia DR3 catalogue.
found: In particular, the pattern observed at R ≲ 5 kpc can be associated with the influence of the Galactic bar.

papers.t: Unsupervised Machine Learning Classification of FRB 20121102A across Distinct Active Episodes: Implications for FRB Emission Physics and Source Environments
papers.status: 16 pages, 2 table, 13 figures. Accepted for publication in ApJ
papers.one: These results suggest that this cluster may represent a distinct burst population potentially associated with different emission physics.
papers.q: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are millisecond-duration radio transients of extragalactic origin. Identifying distinct burst populations and investigating their variations across active episodes provide important insights into the physical origins of repeating FRBs.
papers.how: The abstract does not describe the method in detail.
found: In this paper, we apply an unsupervised machine learning approach to bursts from three active episodes of FRB 20121102A observed by the Five-hundred-metre Aperture Spherical Telescope (FAST).

Notably, Cluster 1 exhibits bimodal-like distributions in central frequency and bandwidth and contains nearly all high-energy bursts, with a mean energy about an order of magnitude higher than those of the other clusters.

papers.t: Receiving Exoplanet Messages with Gravitational-wave Carriers: The Gravitational-wave Radial Velocity Method
papers.status: 21 pages, 7 figures. Published by The Astrophysical Journal. Published in Astrophysical Journal 1012 (2026) pp. 21
papers.one: In this work we show that while similar to electromagnetic-based RV, this GW-based method depends on the ''phase modulation index'' (PMI), a parameter that is more sensitive to high-mass, long-period exoplanets.
papers.q: Gravitational-wave (GW) radial velocity (RV) may offer a new method for detecting exoplanets, one that would primarily target planets orbiting GW-emitting, ultracompact, post-main-sequence stellar objects such as white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes. We investigate the potential of GW RV for GW sources in both the mid-frequency spectrum (where the upcoming LISA mission will operate) and the high-frequency spectrum (where the current LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) observatories operate).
papers.how: The abstract does not describe the method in detail.
found: Remarkably, we find that the PMI increases by a factor of ~O(10⁴ - 10⁶) going from the mid-frequency to the high-frequency GW spectrum, which results in a greater redistribution of observed power due to the exoplanet's presence.

papers.t: Satellite pairs in the Local Group: from spatial clustering to dynamical associations in observations and ΛCDM simulations
papers.by: Mariana P. Júlio, Marcel S. Pawlowski and Noam I. Libeskind
papers.status: Accepted for publication in ApJ on 17-10-2026. 30 pages, 12 figures, 8 tables
papers.one: We identify close nearest-neighbour associations by comparing the observed satellite distributions with isotropic populations that reproduce the radial distributions of each host, and investigate their physical nature using line-of-sight velocities, proper motions, and gravitational binding estimates.
papers.q: Our comparison uses three distinct simulated Local Group analogues drawn from the HESTIA suite, allowing us to assess the observed pair statistics against multiple cosmological realisations of the Local Group environment. We find that the MW exhibits a significant excess of close satellite associations relative to isotropic expectations, with a pairing efficiency of ~53%, nearly twice that found in the simulated analogues (~17-27%).
papers.how: We investigate the incidence and physical nature of satellite galaxy pairs in the Local Group using updated observational data for the Milky Way (MW) and Andromeda (M31), together with analogues from the HESTIA constrained cosmological simulations.
found: This excess persists after applying a stellar mass cut (M⋆> 10⁴ M☉) to match the resolution limits of the simulations.
In contrast, the M31 satellite system is broadly consistent with isotropy, with a pairing efficiency of ~28%.

papers.t: Jet energetics and remnant magnetism in short gamma-ray bursts from binary neutron-star mergers: A statistical study via broadband afterglow modeling
papers.by: Changwen Zeng, Zhiwei Chen, Youjun Lu and 2 others
papers.status: 24 pages, 14 figures; accepted for publication in A&A
papers.one: For the 15 strictly constrained bursts, we find a median Eₖ ≃ 3.8×10⁴⁹ erg and η_γ ≃ 0.35, with respective 68% intervals of [5.1×10⁴⁸,1.9×10⁵⁰] erg and [0.09, 0.79].
papers.q: Short gamma-ray bursts (sGRBs) are believed to originate from compact binary mergers, particularly binary neutron star (BNS) mergers, providing a probe of jet energetics and merger remnants. We derive distributions of beaming-corrected jet kinetic energy Eₖ and radiative efficiency η_γ, and combine these with binary population synthesis and numerical simulations to infer remnant black hole (BH) magnetic fields assuming the Blandford-Znajek (BZ) jet-launching mechanism.
papers.how: We compile broadband afterglow observations of 40 sGRBs and perform forward-shock modeling with off-axis Gaussian jets, excluding data potentially affected by additional energy injection.
found: The inferred magnetic field supplied by the accretion disk and threading the BH horizon is approximately 7×10¹⁵ G, with a 68% credible interval of [2.3×10¹⁵,2.4×10¹⁶] G, depending slightly on the neutron star equation of state.
The full sample yields a higher median field of approximately 2×10¹⁶ G, with the high-energy and high-field tails predominantly contributed by less well-constrained bursts.

papers.t: The Same But Different: SiO₂ Clouds in Two L-Dwarfs with JWST
papers.by: Joshua D. Lothringer, Jeff A. Valenti, Sarah E. Moran and 9 others
papers.status: 36 pages, 13 figures, 12 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJ
papers.one: These results show both the complexity and diversity of brown dwarf cloud properties, while also highlighting the constraining power of broad-wavelength JWST observations of cloudy L-dwarfs.
papers.q: The precision of brown dwarf spectra from JWST enables unprecedented insight into the atmospheric and cloud properties of sub-stellar atmospheres. Here, we compare both self-consistent radiative-convective equilibrium (RCE) and retrieval atmosphere models to high-SNR 1--18~μm spectra of two field L-dwarfs from JWST, J0624 (L5) and J2148 (L6--L6.5).
papers.how: Next, we use petitRADTRANS to retrieve atmosphere and cloud properties, finding strong evidence for the presence of SiO₂ clouds in both objects.
found: Our observations include spectral features from H₂O, CO, CO₂, CH₄, Na, and K and cover approximately 98% of the outgoing thermal emission from the two objects.
We first compare the data to three independent grids of 1D-RCE models: BT-Settl, exoREM, and Sonora Diamondback.

papers.t: Stellar-Field-Driven Induction Heating Unlikely To Cause Significant Heating in Giant Exoplanets
papers.by: Madison Brady, Darryl Z. Seligman and Cassidy Walker
papers.one: However, hot Jupiters with large wind speeds may have high magnetic Reynolds numbers and therefore be in the inductive regime.
papers.q: A planet moving through a changing magnetic field will have a current induced on it by that magnetic field. If the magnetic Reynolds number in the upper atmosphere of this planet is small, the dissipation of this current could result in observable changes to the planet's properties.
papers.how: The abstract does not describe the method in detail.

papers.t: Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit
papers.by: Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, Jason J. Wang, Katherine L. Bouman and 4 others
papers.one: A new way of subtracting a star's glare lets the Webb telescope see planets two to fifteen times fainter than before.
papers.q: To photograph a planet you must remove the light of its star, which is millions of times brighter. The usual method subtracts an image of a reference star, but the telescope flexes slightly between the two exposures and the leftover glare hides faint planets. Can that limit be beaten?
papers.how: They built a physical model of how starlight passes through the telescope and its coronagraph, with millions of adjustable numbers describing the instrument's tiny drifts, and let software tune all of them at once to match the data. They tested it on real Webb NIRCam observations.
found: 2 to 15 times better than standard techniques
the planet 51 Eridani b detected at 4.3 micrometres
papers.why: The authors say the same approach could work on ground telescopes, on the Roman Space Telescope and on the planned Habitable Worlds Observatory, and could relax how rigid those telescopes need to be. Stability is one of the most expensive requirements in building them.
papers.careful: The abstract reports results for one instrument. How well the method transfers to others is a stated hope, not yet a demonstration.

papers.t: Searching for Planets around Altair with JWST/NIRCam
papers.by: Tiffany Meshkat, Charles Beichman, Jorge Llop-Sayson and 13 others
papers.one: Webb looked for giant planets around the bright nearby star Altair and found none, which rules out anything bigger than Saturn beyond ten times the Earth–Sun distance.
papers.q: Altair is one of the nearest and youngest stars in our neighbourhood, and young planets still glow with the heat of their formation. Does it have giant planets, and is it a good target for future imaging?
papers.how: Two sets of Webb images taken with a coronagraph blocking the star, at wavelengths of 2.0 and 4.4 micrometres. A real planet moves across the sky with its star; a background star does not, so the second visit sorts one from the other.
found: 150 billionths of the star's brightness at 2 arcseconds (10 AU)
planets heavier than Jupiter beyond 5 AU, heavier than Saturn beyond 10 AU
several; none moved with Altair, and their colours match background stars
papers.why: A clean non-detection is useful. It tells planet-formation models what this kind of star does not make, and it certifies Altair as a clean reference star for the Roman Space Telescope's coronagraph.
papers.careful: The mass limits depend on models of how bright a young planet of a given mass should be. Planets closer than about 5 AU remain hidden in the star's glare.

papers.t: Planetary material is a major source of hydrogen in helium-atmosphere white dwarfs
papers.by: Paula Izquierdo, Andrew Swan, Christopher J. Manser and 36 others
papers.one: At least a fifth of a certain kind of dead star got some of its hydrogen by swallowing pieces of its own planetary system.
papers.q: Some white dwarfs have atmospheres of nearly pure helium, yet traces of hydrogen show up in them and increase with age. Does that hydrogen float up from inside the star, or does it arrive from outside, in water-bearing asteroids and comets?
papers.how: A simple model that allows both routes, compared with two independent samples of helium-atmosphere white dwarfs from the DESI and Sloan surveys, at temperatures between about 10,000 and 19,000 K.
found: White dwarfs that must have taken in planetary hydrogen
at least 22 ± 2% of those with detectable hydrogen
ices, water-bearing minerals or planetary atmospheres
papers.why: It means the remains of planetary systems are delivering water-rich material to dead stars routinely, not just in a few extreme cases. White dwarfs are the one place where the insides of rocky bodies from other systems can be chemically analysed.
papers.careful: 22% is a lower limit, and the model is deliberately simple.

papers.t: Unidentified Sources in the 4FGL-DR4 Fermi-LAT Catalog as Potential Dark Matter Satellites
papers.by: Fernando Valenciano, Miguel A. Sánchez-Conde and Jorge Martin Camalich
papers.one: None of the 2,428 unexplained gamma-ray sources in the sky looks like a clump of dark matter, and that absence rules out some kinds of dark matter particle.
papers.q: If dark matter is made of WIMPs, pairs of them should occasionally annihilate into gamma rays. The Milky Way's halo should contain small dark clumps with no stars, which would appear as gamma-ray sources with nothing else there. Are any of the Fermi telescope's unidentified sources such clumps?
papers.how: They started from the 2,428 sources in Fermi's 14-year catalogue that match no known object, filtered out those that cannot be dark clumps (wrong spectrum, variable, extended in the wrong way), and analysed the spectra of the rest in detail.
found: within a factor of 2 to 3 of the benchmark 'thermal relic' annihilation rate at the lowest masses
thermal WIMPs lighter than about 50 GeV annihilating to bottom quarks
papers.why: This is an independent check on the limits from dwarf galaxies, using a population of objects that cannot be studied any other way.
papers.careful: The limits depend on predictions of how many dark clumps the halo holds and how bright they would be, which come from simulations.

papers.t: Accretion variability as a probe of black holes and their environments: Light curve signatures of a single hot spot
papers.by: I. Urso, C. Deffayet, A. Held and F. H. Vincent
papers.one: The flicker of gas near a black hole carries a fingerprint of how the hole bends light, and this paper works out what to look for.
papers.q: A bright clump of gas orbiting close to a black hole brightens and fades as it circles. How much of that flicker comes from the clump itself and how much from the warped spacetime its light crosses on the way to us?
papers.how: Simulated movies of a single flickering hot spot, with its light traced to a distant observer three ways: through flat space, around a non-rotating black hole and around a spinning one. They compared the brightness records and their frequency content.
found: reproduces the main features at moderate viewing angles
in how different parts of the image vary relative to one another, which encodes orientation and lensing
papers.why: The black hole at the centre of the Milky Way flares several times a day. Timing signatures like these are a way to test gravity there without resolving an image.
papers.careful: The abstract gives no numbers, and the authors say more work is needed to see whether the conclusions hold for realistic discs and not just one idealised spot.

papers.t: Spacetime contactability in Galactic civilization networks: Contact counts and percolation
papers.status: 24 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to Acta Astronautica
papers.one: If civilisations come and go at different times, a galaxy could be full of one-way messages even though almost no one ever gets a reply.
papers.q: Estimates of how many civilisations we might hear usually assume they all exist at once. Signals travel at the speed of light and civilisations have lifetimes, so who can actually hear whom, and can a network of contact form?
papers.how: Mathematics, not observation. The author derives how many others a civilisation hears over its lifetime, and the threshold at which contacts link into a connected network, then applies it to a disc shaped like the Milky Way.
found: Average number heard over a lifetime
twice a single 'contactability' number, whatever the timing
drops from 4.51 when all exist at once to 1.32 when lifetimes are short compared with travel times
Upper bound from our silence so far
a civilisation at the Sun's position would hear at most 5.5 others on average
complete exchanges become rare once signals take longer than lifetimes
papers.why: It reframes the silence: hearing nothing back is expected even in a populated galaxy. It is also a nice application of one-way light time to a question people care about.
papers.careful: This is a model built on assumptions nobody can test yet, and the bound assumes an ideal complete survey. It has not been peer reviewed.

papers.t: Comprehensive Visible and Near-infrared Keck and Gemini Monitoring and Characterization of Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS during its Encounter with the Solar System
papers.by: Bryce T. Bolin, Jeffrey Cooke, Brian C. Lemaux and 43 others
papers.status: 53 pages, 21 figures, 9 tables. Submitted to AJ
papers.one: Ten months of observations of the third known visitor from another star, from its approach to its departure.
papers.q: 3I/ATLAS formed around another star. As it passed through the Solar System, how did its colour, dust and gas change, and how does it compare with our own comets?
papers.how: Images and spectra from the Keck and Gemini telescopes on 28 occasions between July 2025 and May 2026, in visible and near-infrared light, covering the passage around the Sun.
found: did not change significantly from before to after its closest approach to the Sun
fell faster on the way out than it rose on the way in
2.7 to 10 billion kg, depending on the assumed dust speed
the ratio of C₂ to CN nearly doubled between September and November 2025
no absorption that survives every calibration they tried
papers.why: It is a complete before-and-after record of material from another planetary system being heated by a star for possibly the first time in billions of years, and a benchmark for the next interstellar visitor.
papers.careful: The mass figures depend on assumed grain sizes and the size of the nucleus. The paper is submitted, not yet reviewed.

papers.t: Three subpopulations of binary black holes in mass, spin magnitudes and tilts following GWTC-5
papers.by: Asad Hussain, Maximiliano Isi and Aaron Zimmerman
papers.one: The 259 black hole mergers detected so far seem to fall into three families, told apart by how fast the black holes spin.
papers.q: Pairs of black holes can form in more than one way: from two stars born together, or from black holes that meet in a crowded cluster, some of them products of earlier mergers. Each route should leave a mark on the masses and spins. Can the catalogue be sorted that way?
papers.how: A statistical model that lets the data divide itself into groups, each with its own pattern of mass ratio, spin and spin direction, applied to the 259 mergers in the fifth LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA catalogue.
found: dominates near 35 solar masses; both holes barely spin; nearly equal masses
about half the pairs near 10 solar masses; spins about 0.2, roughly aligned with the orbit
dominates above 60 solar masses; the heavier hole spins at about 0.7, pointing in any direction
papers.why: Fast, randomly tilted spins in the heaviest pairs are what you expect if those black holes were themselves made in earlier mergers. The result adds to the evidence that the detectors are seeing more than one origin story.
papers.careful: The families come from a flexible statistical model; the abstract does not tie each to a specific formation route. Not yet peer reviewed.
